content: The regulation of prosthetic and orthotic products is essential to ensuring access to safe, effective, and high-quality devices. As these are health-related products, it is most effective to integrate their regulation, including the components and materials used, into the national healthcare regulatory system. Additionally, clinical field tests can confirm that these products are suitable for their intended purpose. National regulation of prosthetic and orthotic products, components, and materials should be a core part of the national healthcare regulatory framework. These products must undergo structural testing to meet ISO or equivalent standards before being marketed. Research and development in prosthetics and orthotics are critical for advancing technical and clinical innovations, improving cost-effectiveness, and ensuring the quality of treatments. However, there is a significant lack of evidence regarding the appropriateness, effectiveness, and cost-efficiency of technologies and methods in this field. More national and international research is needed to advance practices and services. A major limitation is the insufficient training of prosthetists and orthotists in conducting research. Countries should encourage research and train professionals to conduct studies, share findings, and apply them in practice. To increase access to prosthetic and orthotic services in resource-limited settings, there is a need for affordable, mass-produced products that are cost-effective, quality-controlled, and context-appropriate. Despite technical advances, the availability of these products remains limited in lowand middle-income countries. Governments must work with national and international stakeholders, including private industry and targeted international funding, to make these products more accessible and affordable. Clinical and technical research in prosthetics and orthotics should be conducted and shared both nationally and globally. Affordable, high-quality, and context-appropriate prosthetic and orthotic products should be developed and made widely available. Proper assessment and attention to user needs during the design process can provide effective solutions for complex cases. Prosthetics and orthotics services should be delivered by competent, adequately trained professionals. Complex cases require a multidisciplinary team with complementary skills to provide effective treatment. Training in prosthetics and orthotics should align with national and international educational standards and be available at various levels to meet national needs. Continuing professional development (CPD) is essential for maintaining and improving the quality of services, especially in evolving fields. Workforce planning is critical to ensuring the availability of the right personnel in the right locations. This involves assessing the demand for personnel, comparing it with the existing supply, and identifying training needs. Each service delivery unit should have at least one experienced prosthetist or orthotist to supervise and guide clinical and technical work. State regulation of prosthetists and orthotists is necessary to enforce accountability and reduce the risk of harm to users. Professional recognition enhances the status of these personnel and the services they provide, motivating them and improving service provision. Prosthetists and orthotists should assume responsibility for the services provided by associate and non-clinical personnel under their supervision. Prosthetics and orthotics services should embody the principles of user-centered care, ensuring that users can make informed decisions about their care and receive services that respect their dignity, choices, and rights. Service providers must share information about assessment results and treatment options with users and caregivers to enable informed decision-making. A documented user policy, developed collaboratively by users, caregivers, and providers, safeguards user rights and reinforces user-centered practices. Access to prosthetics and orthotics services is inequitable in many countries, despite the principle of equal access to healthcare. These services should be available to all individuals based on their needs and choices, without discrimination. Strong coordination between prosthetics and orthotics services and other health and rehabilitation sectors is essential for inclusive healthcare. A three-tier system with differentiated services at primary, secondary, and tertiary levels can improve access, especially in rural areas. Decentralizing services through satellite and mobile units or community-based programs can further enhance access. Readily accessible maintenance and repair services are crucial for ensuring the optimal functioning and longevity of prosthetic and orthotic products, reducing the need for frequent replacements and increasing cost-effectiveness.
